ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with a long, formal presentation style during talks and much briefer, conversational exchanges before and after. Openings are informal and chatty, full of greetings, logistical checks, light teasing, and repeated acknowledgments like “yeah,” “okay,” and “great.” Speech is highly disfluent and spontaneous: speakers use fillers (“um,” “uh”), repetitions, self-corrections, false starts, and unfinished phrasing, especially in questions. Overlap and interruptions are fairly common but cooperative rather than competitive; people jump in with quick confirmations, clarifications, or follow-up questions. The tone is collegial and moderately informal despite technical discussion, with praise preceding questions (“great talk,” “beautiful work”) and disagreement or uncertainty framed indirectly through hedges such as “I think,” “maybe,” “it could be,” “I’m not sure,” and “do you feel like.” Participants build on prior comments by restating part of the answer, connecting it to related work, or widening the question. Questions are often prefaced as “quick,” “naive,” or “a couple of questions,” and tend to be exploratory, multipart, and conversational rather than sharply challenging.

Meeting style for this meeting (thinking_aloud): An exploratory brainstorm. People ask questions they don't know the answer to, try out half-formed ideas, and sometimes contradict themselves. Nothing is decided. Turns are short to medium and often end in a question.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - I wonder if it's even the same thing- like, are we measuring the same thing in both places?
  - Honestly no idea. Maybe? I'd have to look at how they set it up.
  - Huh. Okay, so what if we just asked them?
Opening: Start with one person apologizing for being a couple of minutes late and asking where the group has got to.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Assessing whether forest carbon credits actually protect forest and who gets to decide how that is measured.

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Okafor
speakers.background: A forest ecologist and geospatial research engineer with 11 years of experience evaluating REDD+ and improved-forest-management claims across tropical and temperate forests. She builds reproducible monitoring pipelines that combine Landsat and Sentinel time series, airborne data where available, stratified field inventories, and uncertainty propagation. Her prior work has examined baseline inflation, spatial leakage into neighboring areas, degradation missed by canopy-cover products, and reversal risk from fire, harvesting, and land-use change.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Amina treats a credit as an empirical claim about avoided or removed emissions, not evidence in itself. Her opening question is: "Did credited protection produce a real, additional, and durable difference in forest carbon relative to a defensible counterfactual baseline, once leakage, measurement uncertainty, and permanence risk are accounted for?" She wants case comparisons that test project claims against independently constructed reference areas and inventory evidence where access permits. She accepts that governance shapes outcomes and data availability, but insists that causal ecological inference cannot be substituted with documentation or institutional legitimacy.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Mateo R. Quispe
speakers.background: A fourth-year PhD candidate in comparative environmental politics with six years of fieldwork and policy research on forest governance in Latin America and Southeast Asia. He uses process tracing, document analysis, semi-structured interviews, and comparative case-study design to study land tenure, decentralization, enforcement, and benefit-sharing arrangements. He has worked with municipal agencies, customary land institutions, and national forestry authorities, with particular attention to how formal rules interact with locally recognized claims to land and forest use.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mateo approaches carbon projects as arrangements of authority rather than simply technical interventions. His opening question is: "Who has the recognized and practical authority to set rules, control land, monitor compliance, distribute benefits, and enforce restrictions in carbon-credit projects—and how do state, local, and community authorities shape whether those rules hold?" He wants to trace tenure histories, overlapping jurisdictions, enforcement capacity, and contestation around project boundaries. He expects ecological outcomes to be inseparable from whether people view project rules as legitimate and whether institutions can act on them, while remaining alert to the possibility that formal authority and on-the-ground authority diverge.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
speakers.background: An STS scholar and principal investigator with 17 years of research on environmental quantification, standards, and global climate governance. Her work combines ethnographic observation, interviews, archival analysis, and close reading of methodologies, validation reports, audit trails, and registry records. She has studied how satellite classifications, carbon-accounting protocols, verification practices, and expert judgment turn heterogeneous forests and social relations into comparable units for markets and regulation.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Leila examines credits as produced through sociotechnical practices of measurement and authorization. Her opening question is: "How are claims about forest protection translated into tradable carbon credits through methodologies, baselines, data infrastructures, auditors, certifiers, and registries—and whose knowledge is accepted, excluded, or rendered legible in that process?" She is interested in how a methodology defines what counts as a forest, a threat, a valid counterfactual, and credible evidence, and how these choices distribute authority. She will help the group formulate a bridging question around the relationship between observed forest-protection outcomes and the institutions and measurement practices that define and authorize credits, without presuming a single metric or method. She supports selecting comparative cases only after data access and permissions have been confirmed.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a first scoping meeting with one ecologist, one political scientist, and one STS scholar. Each participant must open by stating a distinct research question. The ecologist's question must concern whether credited forest protection is real, using counterfactual baselines, leakage, forest inventory or remote sensing, and permanence. The political scientist's question must concern who has authority to govern and enforce projects, including land tenure and relations among state, local, and community authorities. The STS scholar's question must concern how ecological claims are transformed into tradable credits, including methodologies, auditors, certifiers, and whose knowledge is treated as valid. The discussion should identify a plausible shared bridging question about the relationship between forest-protection outcomes and the institutions and measurement practices that define and authorize credits. Do not force agreement on a single metric or method. The team may agree that the comparative cases will be selected after confirming data access and permissions; this remains unresolved. No participant should be asked to solve the synthesis on behalf of the assistant.

ground_truth.bridging_question: How do ecological measurement choices and the governance arrangements that authorize them shape both whether forest carbon projects deliver durable, non-displaced forest protection and whose knowledge and authority determine that claim?

disciplinary_subquestions.ecology: Compared with a credible counterfactual, do credited projects produce durable reductions in forest loss or emissions, accounting for baseline construction, leakage, forest condition, and permanence?

disciplinary_subquestions.science_and_technology_studies: How are baseline, monitoring, and uncertainty judgments converted into credits through project methodologies, auditors, and certifiers, and which forms of local, technical, and institutional knowledge are recognized or excluded?

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: Sorry, I’m a couple of minutes late—where have we got to? Oh, we haven’t started, great. I was hoping today we could get a feel for what a joint question might be. Not just whether these projects protect forest, but how that protection gets turned into an authorized credit in the first place, and what we’d actually need access to before choosing cases.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: Mm, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: I'd start one layer earlier than the credit. Did the project actually change forest carbon compared with a plausible no-project trajectory? And then, because Leila's right, we can ask how that empirical claim became auditable and authorized. But before we choose regions, I really need to know if we can get comparable boundary files, cloud-free time series, and at least some inventory access. Otherwise, we may be- we may be comparing paperwork rather than outcomes.

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: Exactly, I’d hate for the comparison to turn into a comparison of what just happened to be documented. Amina, a quick question. In the products these projects typically use, what kinds of carbon-relevant change are most likely to— I’m losing the thread. Like degradation under canopy, selective logging, that sort of thing, what’s most likely to disappear from view? Because that may be where the formal monitoring chain and people’s accounts start diverging.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Exactly. Optical canopy-loss products are weakest for low-intensity selective logging, understory fire, edge degradation, and gradual biomass depletion where the crown layer still looks intact. We'd want dense Landsat–Sentinel trajectories. Probably radar in the humid sites and repeat plots or airborne structure data if anybody will release them. Otherwise a stable canopy series can- it can conceal a carbon stock that's very much not stable.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: That's useful, because the places where the canopy looks stable may be exactly where a developer or district office can say enforcement worked, while people describe very different use rules underneath it. Amina, would the choice of reference area also get shaky if neighboring communities have different road access or, um, if one has a patrol arrangement the other doesn't? That seems less like background noise and more like part of the project's governing landscape.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: If road access, patrols, or market exposure differ, that affects both treatment assignment and what the counterfactual would likely be. So a nearby unprotected polygon isn't automatically a valid control. We'd need to match on those drivers, ideally on pre-project disturbance trajectories too, and explicitly map any extraction that's displaced across the boundary. Mateo, how visible are those patrol arrangements in local records versus just in people's accounts, because that could...

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: Mostly, if they exist at all, they'll be patchy. Patrol logs and municipal reports usually record planned rounds or incidents, but the discretionary part, who gets warned, who can negotiate access, whose harvesting gets treated as a violation, that usually only comes out in interviews, and the accounts may conflict. I'd treat that mismatch as evidence, not just use the paperwork to validate one version. Could your spatial analysis detect whether pressure shifts into particular customary-use areas, even when those boundaries aren't on the official maps, or...

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: Hm, that's important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Potentially, yes, but only if we can get those customary-use areas carefully enough to georeference them without acting like the edges are fixed. We could look for local differences in disturbance or biomass proxies on the other side of a project boundary, then use the interview accounts to interpret whether that's displacement rather than, say, a road effect. But I wouldn't call it leakage from pixels alone.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: Yeah, cautiously, I think.

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: And that caution is kind of the bridge, isn't it? We may find a spatial pattern, but calling it leakage- calling it leakage only becomes official through a methodology's boundary rules and evidence thresholds. I'm wondering, Mateo, when customary areas can't safely be mapped precisely, what would be a responsible way to carry that knowledge into the comparison without forcing people to disclose more than they want?

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: I think we can use graduated disclosure instead of one map. People can identify broad zones, routes, or relationships to the project boundary without giving us household-level sites or a definitive customary line. And we should separate what they tell us for analysis from what appears in a case report, especially if a disputed area could trigger enforcement. Would your audit materials recognize that kind of deliberately imprecise evidence, Leila, or does it effectively disappear?

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: Often it effectively disappears, unless the standard has a category for it. And most of these protocols want a location, a date, a source, something an auditor can tick through. But that's exactly- precisely what seems worth tracing, whether imprecision gets treated as a legitimate protection practice or just downgraded to "anecdotal." I've seen two pretty similar audit files handle local testimony completely differently, and I still don't know what drove that distinction.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: That variation itself is a governance question, I think. If one testimony becomes auditable because it has a named representative, a GPS point, or it fits the consultation template, and another gets excluded because disclosure would create risk, then the credit is partly built on an unequal evidentiary rule. In interviews, I’d want to ask who was able to speak, who could contest the record afterward, and whether there was any consequence when they disagreed...

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: Maybe our joint question has to keep that asymmetry visible, not just whether forest change occurred, but how particular observations and voices become eligible to establish it. I’d be very interested in whether the validation and verification records let us see any challenge process at all. Like, when a consultation account conflicts with a baseline or monitoring claim, where does that disagreement actually go?

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: I’d be careful not to assume the formal grievance channel is the only place disagreement goes. In some settings, people contest through municipal offices, customary leaders, or just noncompliance, and none of that may enter a verification file. Could we trace a few specific disputed claims from the consultation meeting through the developer, the auditor, and- whatever local forum people actually used?

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: I like that much more than treating “the community view” as one input. We could follow a small number of claims as they change form, from a spoken concern to a meeting minute, a developer response, an audit finding, a registry record, and also notice where the trail just stops. Though we'd need permission, and we'd need to be careful not to make a dispute more visible than the people involved want.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: For me, those claim-traces should sit alongside a trace of the baseline itself, like which deforestation-risk assumptions survived review, which contrary observations were excluded or unresolved, and whether that changes the quantified counterfactual. Leila, in the files you've seen, do auditors leave enough of a trail to reconstruct that, or do we only- do we just see the final approved baseline?

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: Sometimes, but it’s uneven. Validation reports often keep the headline challenge and the auditor’s resolution, but the working exchanges, rejected attachments, and the reasons a contrary observation was judged insufficient are much harder to get. Sometimes they’re with the developer, and sometimes they’re not retained in the public file at all. So case selection has to include whether we can get at least some version history or correspondence. Otherwise, we’ll mistake a finalized baseline for an uncontested one.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Then I’d make version history and raw monitoring inputs a hard feasibility screen, not just a nice-to-have. A public PDD plus a polished validation report can’t tell us whether the credited counterfactual survived serious challenge, and without boundary files and enough cloud-free or radar coverage, we can’t independently test the outcome side either. We may end up with fewer candidate cases, but I think that’s better- preferable to a comparison where uncertainty is structurally invisible.

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: Hard screens, but perhaps we should also record who controls access to each missing layer. The absence of correspondence or raw inputs isn't just a limitation on us. It may tell us something about how challenge is made untraceable. Could we make a short candidate-case matrix that distinguishes records that are genuinely unavailable from records we're simply not permitted to see, before we settle on the two regions?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: And the matrix needs a separate column for ecological comparability, not just access. Boundary geometry, project start date, pre-treatment imagery, cloud burden, radar availability, and whether inventories are independent or project-managed. Otherwise we could select two beautifully documented cases where one just, just isn't estimable at the carbon-stock level.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: Okay, and tenure access too.

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: Tenure access has to be in there, not just whether we can interview people, but whether we can see the permits, overlapping claims, and the records that show who was recognized as entitled to consent or receive benefits. Otherwise, we could read a consultation file as representative when the relevant authority had already been, um, narrowed before anyone got into the room. Maybe the matrix needs a column for that chain of recognition, even if it's partly unknown at first.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: Yeah—especially who gets recognized before consultation even begins.

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: We’re at time, but that feels like the right place to stop. The recognized claimant, the recognized evidence, and the recognized forest boundary may all be set upstream of the credit calculation. Let’s just use that as a, um, prompt for the candidate matrix rather than pretending we’ve resolved it today.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Quispe
transcript.text: Okay, I should let everyone go. I’ll leave it there and, and follow up by email. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Great, bye—talk soon.

transcript.speaker: Professor Leila S. Banerjee
transcript.text: Thanks, both—really helpful. Bye.
